title: Pods as Workers, Not Agents: Rethinking the Deployment Unit for AI Agents on Kubernetes
gist: Drawing on the kagent project, CNCF's Lin Sun argues the Kubernetes Pod remains the right execution unit for AI agents but the wrong deployment, identity, and lifecycle unit, and that Google's Agent Substrate control plane — which decouples logical 'Actors' from a fixed pool of long-lived Pods — points to where agent infrastructure is heading.

themes.theme: Why Pods Don't Fit Agent Lifecycles

insights.claim: Lin Sun, drawing on the kagent project in a CNCF blog post, argues the Kubernetes Pod is the right execution unit for an agent but is no longer the right deployment, identity, or lifecycle unit.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Platform teams building agent infrastructure should decouple 'where code executes' from 'what owns identity and lifecycle' as a core design principle rather than assuming Kubernetes-native microservice patterns transfer directly.
insights.locator: In a CNCF blog post, Lin Sun draws on work in the kagent project

insights.claim: Questions about isolating agents from each other, giving each its own identity, enforcing access and network policy, observing individual agent activity, and assigning multi-tenant ownership are agent-platform questions rather than Kubernetes questions, even though Kubernetes is where the answers must ultimately be expressed.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Clarifies where solution effort belongs: building a separate agent-platform control layer, not stretching native Kubernetes primitives to answer questions they weren't designed for.
insights.locator: The questions that surface once agent counts grow are familiar

insights.claim: Unlike microservices expected to be continuously available, an AI agent may wake only when assigned a task, run for seconds or minutes, then sit idle, may spawn subagents to run subtasks in parallel, and may pause indefinitely awaiting human approval — making a dedicated always-on Pod per potential agent wasteful.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Directly undermines the naive design of provisioning one persistent Pod per agent; teams estimating compute cost for agent fleets should model bursty, idle-heavy usage rather than always-on microservice cost curves.
insights.locator: The difficulty is that agents do not behave like the microservices

themes.theme: kagent's Evolution from Naive to Isolated

insights.claim: kagent originally ran many agents inside a single runtime, then moved to making each agent a first-class Kubernetes workload with its own Pod, Service, and ServiceAccount, gaining process/container isolation, ServiceAccount identity tied into existing auth, native network/admission policy enforcement, per-agent log/metric/trace attribution, and Kubernetes-native scheduling.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Documents a naive-to-mature evolution path (shared runtime to per-agent Pod) that other teams building agent infrastructure will likely repeat, giving them a shortcut past the first mistake.
insights.locator: This is the approach kagent adopted after initially running many agents

insights.claim: kagent subsequently added stronger isolation through the Kubernetes Agent Sandbox project, on top of its per-agent Pod model.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Shows isolation requirements for agents keep escalating even after basic per-agent Pod isolation, a maturity curve worth tracking in agent-infra tooling.
insights.locator: kagent subsequently added support for stronger isolation

themes.theme: Agent Substrate as the Control-Plane Layer

insights.claim: Google's Agent Substrate, introduced alongside Agent Sandbox, adds a control plane above Kubernetes: Agent Sandbox provides isolated execution environments while Agent Substrate manages placement of logical agents onto and between workers, letting a fixed pool of long-lived Pods support far more logical agents than a dedicated, continuously running Pod per agent would allow.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Signals where the agent-infrastructure market is heading — a decoupled control-plane layer above Kubernetes — with Google positioned as an early mover worth watching for tooling and vendor plays.
insights.locator: Another approach is to stop treating each agent as a Kubernetes workload

insights.claim: Agent Substrate's abstractions mirror familiar platform-engineering concepts: a WorkerPool is analogous to a NodePool, Workers to Nodes, and an ActorTemplate to the declarative specification of a Pod; Kubernetes is aware only of WorkerPools and ActorTemplates, while Workers and Actors live in Agent Substrate's own CLI and API, with each Worker mapped to a single Pod.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Gives platform engineers a concrete abstraction map for evaluating or building a similar agent control-plane layer without having to reverse-engineer Google's design from scratch.
insights.locator: Its abstractions mirror concepts platform engineers already know

insights.claim: An Actor — the entity that acts as an AI agent in Agent Substrate — is a logical unit scheduled onto a Worker when work arrives and suspended, resumed, or removed as its lifecycle requires, rather than being permanently bound to one Pod.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Confirms the core mechanism enabling many-to-one agent-to-Pod density, the efficiency claim underlying the whole architecture shift.
insights.locator: An Actor, the entity that "acts as" an AI agent

insights.claim: Because an Actor can run on any Worker, identity may need to belong to the ActorTemplate, namespace, tenant, and version rather than to a Pod or Service, with access control, network policy, and runtime permissions expressed at the template level with per-Actor overrides.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Implies existing IAM and network-policy tooling built around Pod-level identity needs rework for agent fleets, a real integration cost security and platform teams should budget for when adopting this pattern.
insights.locator: Sun argues that if an Actor can run on any Worker

insights.claim: Once execution is no longer one-to-one with Pods, ownership, quotas, and billing become harder to reason about, and observability must follow the logical Actor wherever it is scheduled rather than a fixed Pod, associating logs, traces, and audit records with the Actor itself.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Flags a concrete gap for FinOps and observability tooling vendors: cost attribution and tracing built for static Pod identity will need new instrumentation for agent workloads that migrate across Workers.
insights.locator: Ownership, quotas, and billing become harder to reason about

insights.claim: The open question Sun raises is narrow: not whether Kubernetes remains the industry standard for microservices and inference workloads at scale (it does), but whether the Pod, having proved itself as an execution environment, should also remain the unit of deployment, identity, and lifecycle specifically for AI agents.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Useful framing when evaluating vendor claims of 'Kubernetes killers' for agent workloads — this is an additive control-plane layer on top of Kubernetes, not a replacement narrative.
